packages/govee/src/actions.ts.content: The unarmed flash never powers the unit on before sending white `colorwc`. The restore branch is explicitly written for an off unit (`else if (!observed.onOff) { ... turnCommand(false) }`), which only makes sense if the flash turned it on first — but no `turnCommand(true)` is sent. On a unit that is currently off, `colorwc` alone does not light it (the transport in `govee-lan.ts` sends `turn(true)` before the white `colorwc` for exactly this reason), so IDENTIFY produces no visible flash and the user cannot identify/name the unit; the subsequent `turn(false)` restore is then a no-op. Add a power-on before the white command (mirroring the production transport), which the off-state restore already compensates for.

The flash is performed and then restored as a single unguarded sequence. If any `sendRaw`/`sendJson`/`wait(options.flashMs)` rejects (a `Waiter` that rejects, a transport error, or a `paint()` RangeError from a malformed `currentFrame` or `zones > 255`), control jumps out of `identify` and the restore step never runs, leaving the unit stuck in white RGB — the exact state the function's contract promises to undo. Wrap the flash+restore in `try { ... } finally { restore }` so the previous look is re-applied on every exit path.

The stream-vs-`colorwc` path and the restore strategy are chosen from `fixture.armed`, a snapshot taken by the caller before this call. If the unit's real armed state has changed (e.g. a show opened/closed between snapshot and action), the unarmed branch will send a white `colorwc` — and the off-state restore sends `turnCommand(false)` — while the channel is actually armed. Both are documented as capable of terminating the razer channel, which is the data-loss case the module header warns about. Re-confirm armed state at action time (read B2 status, or take the live stream/`armed` value) before deciding the path instead of trusting the stale boolean.

packages/govee/src/actions.ts.content: `testChase` never restores the look that preceded it. In the single-zone unarmed branch the ramp ends on `colorwc(255,255,255)`, i.e. the fixture is left at full white indefinitely; the segmented branch leaves the last travel frame (only one zone lit) on the unit. Unlike `identify`, there is no read-back/restore and no blackout, so the previous static look is lost after every test chase unless the caller re-paints. Consider capturing the pre-chase state (or re-sending a blackout/last known frame) at the end of the walk as `identify` does.

`zones` here is `Math.max(1, fixture.zones)` without flooring, while `chaseFrames` floors internally (`Math.max(1, Math.floor(zones))`). For a non-integer zone count the frame loop uses the floored count but `zoneOrder` is computed with the raw value, so the reported zone order drifts from the bytes actually sent (e.g. reverse step yields `3.5`). There is also no bound check: a zone count > 255 makes `paint` throw `RangeError`, aborting the chase mid-walk. Floor/validate `zones` once and use the same value for both the frames and `zoneOrder`.

When the pre-flash read-back times out, no restore is issued at all and `restored` is `"no-read-back"`, so the unit is left permanently at `colorwc(255,255,255)` (full white) — contradicting the function's stated contract to restore the previous look. A slow/silent unit therefore ends up visibly white until the next command. At minimum this should be surfaced/compensated (e.g. a deterministic blackout or the last known frame) rather than silently leaving the fixture white; document the trade-off if it is intentional.

`restoreFrame` (`fixture.currentFrame`) is passed straight to `paint` with no length check. The flash was sent with `zones` segments, but `paint` derives its segment count from `restoreFrame.length / 3`, so a frame captured at a different resolution paints a different number of zones than the flash (and a length not divisible by 3 throws `RangeError`, leaving the unit white). Guard that `restoreFrame.length === zones * 3` and fall back to the blackout frame otherwise, as the production transport does.

packages/show-planner/src/events.ts.content: When `eventConfidenceFloor` resolves to 0 (`eventMinConfidence[type] === 0`, or a config with `defaultEventConfidence: 0`), the gate `confidence < floor * 0.5` becomes `confidence < 0`, which is never true, and `soft = confidence < floor` is always false. A confidence-0 `drop`/`final-hit` is then emitted as a full impact with no low-confidence downgrade — exactly the case the design says must never happen. Guard against non-positive floors (fall back to a sane floor) instead of letting a 0 silently disable gating.

The moved-event lookup key `${ev.type}@${ev.beat}` is not unique: if `track.musicalEvents` contains two events with the same `type` and `beat` (duplicate detections / multiple detectors reporting the same hit), a single move offset from `movedEvents` is applied to all of them, and a move intended for one is silently lost for the other. Floating-point `beat` formatting also makes the key fragile to precision differences between producer and consumer. Key move offsets on a stable per-event identifier (or index) rather than a `type@beat` string.

packages/show-planner/src/types.ts.content: `mulberry32` derives its state from `parseInt(seedHex.slice(0, 8), 16)`. For any seed whose first 8 chars are not valid hex (e.g. the caller in recurrence.ts passes `` `motif-${seedHex}` ``, and `CompileInput.seedOverride` / `trackFingerprint`'s "id" branch can pass arbitrary strings), `parseInt` returns `NaN` and `NaN >>> 0` is `0`. Every such seed therefore silently collapses to the SAME PRNG stream, defeating seed determinism and masking malformed seed input. Derive the state from a hash of the full input string (e.g. `fnv1aHex(seedHex)`) or validate and throw on a non-hex seed instead of silently falling back to 0.

`envelopeToBeats` silently returns `0` when `bpm <= 0`, and it never guards negative `e.beats`/`e.ms`. An invalid tempo or malformed envelope thus yields a zero (or negative, for the `beats` branch and negative `ms`) sub-beat duration instead of surfacing an error, propagating bad timing into compiled plans and hidden reproducibility failures. Consider throwing (or returning `NaN`) on invalid tempo and validating non-negative inputs at the boundary.

Both `stableStringify` and `canonical` collapse structurally different values into the same string: `undefined`/`NaN`/`Infinity` serialize like `null`, and Map/Set/Date/class instances with no enumerable own keys serialize like `{}`. Since these feed `hashValue`/`stableHash` (and thus style/venue/config hashes and the deterministic compile seed), different inputs can hash identically and reuse the wrong cache entry. Distinguish `undefined`/`null` and handle/serialize Map/Set/Date explicitly (or reject unsupported types).

packages/show-planner/src/types.ts.content: `selectorName` concatenates child names with bare `+`/`&`/`-` and no grouping or escaping, so distinct selector trees map to the same string (e.g. a group literally named `"a+b"` collides with `union(group a, group b)`; nested combinators also flatten ambiguously, and `difference` with more than two operands has no defined meaning). Since this name is used as an identity/lookup key, such collisions can mis-associate or shadow selectors. Wrap each child in parentheses/escaping (or return a structural representation) so the encoding is injective.

`DEVICE_REF` hardcodes specific vendor model IDs (`H6076`, `H1A45`, `segment...=`), which is brittle: new/unlisted device identifiers pass the guard, so this allowlist-style blocklist cannot enforce the 'never device IDs' contract. Conversely, the IPv4 alternative `(?:\d{1,3}\.){3}\d{1,3}` has no boundary/range validation and will false-positive on version-like or dotted numeric tokens (e.g. `v1.2.3.4`, `999.999.999.999`), rejecting valid selectors. Prefer structural validation (reject unknown numeric/ID-like tokens) or add word boundaries and per-octet range checks rather than enumerating specific model numbers.

analysis/src/autolight_analysis/protocol.content: If `os.dup2(2, 1)` fails the failure is silently swallowed, leaving fd 1 still connected to the protocol channel while the function reports success. Third-party C-level prints (HuggingFace progress, native libs) would then write directly into the frame stream and corrupt it. At minimum log the failure (via `log_event`) or surface it, since the whole stdout-discipline guarantee depends on this step.

`start()` is not synchronized and never assigns `_thread` before spawning, so two concurrent `start()` calls each observe `_thread is None` and spawn duplicate heartbeat threads. Also, once `stop()` has been called `_thread` stays non-None, so a subsequent `start()` silently no-ops (heartbeat can never be restarted). Guard the check/set with a lock and reset `_thread` on stop, or document/enforce single-shot lifecycle.

`stop()` only sets the event and does not join the heartbeat thread, so it returns while the thread may still be mid-write; callers cannot know the heartbeat has actually ceased (e.g. before shutting down the writer/process). Consider `self._thread.join(timeout=...)` and clearing `_thread` after stop.
